title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you persuaded someone without authority"?
description: How to answer persuasion and influence questions in consulting interviews, with weak and strong examples and what interviewers look for.
hook: Consultants spend their days persuading people they do not manage, including senior clients. This question tests whether you can understand another person's position and change their mind with care, not pressure.
body:
The question

Tell me about a time you persuaded someone without having authority over them.

A weak answer

I had to convince my manager to use my idea. I explained it really clearly and showed him it was better, and eventually he agreed.

Why it falls short: No detail about the other person's view, no method beyond "explaining clearly", and no result.

A strong answer

Our operations lead didn't want to change the delivery schedule I was proposing, even though it would save money. Instead of pushing, I asked what worried him. It turned out late deliveries had hurt his team's reviews before. So I proposed a two-week trial on one route, with him choosing the route and setting what counted as success. Deliveries stayed on time and costs fell 8%, and he presented the results to his director himself. The change went to every route the next month.

Why it works: It shows listening, understanding the other side, reducing their risk and giving them ownership, with a clear outcome.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Tell me about a time you persuaded someone without having authority over them" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Prove that you understood the other person's objection

Influencing without authority often means helping someone make a decision they initially resist. The story is weaker if the other person agrees immediately after your first slide. Describe what mattered to them, not just how polished your argument was.

In a fictional operations project, a candidate proposed that warehouse staff scan parcels at an additional handoff. The shift manager opposed the idea because the team was already under pressure to meet throughput targets. Rather than repeating that the scan would improve data quality, the candidate observed the handoff and found that the manual search for missing parcels was consuming time later in the day. They proposed a two-day test with one shift, agreed to stop if throughput fell, and tracked both parcels per hour and missing-parcel incidents. The pilot reduced the error rate from 3.0% to 1.2% without a material change in throughput. The manager supported a wider rollout.

The point is the sequence: listen to the objection → identify shared measures → lower the risk of trying the idea → let evidence change the decision. If no measurable outcome exists in your real story, explain what observable behaviour changed instead.

Expect questions such as "What would you have done if the pilot had failed?", "Did the manager have a legitimate concern?" and "How did you avoid making them feel overruled?" Strong persuasion balances conviction with a willingness to update the plan.
